flashcards.question: What is milk and what is the chemical composition of cow's milk?
flashcards.answer:
Milk: a biological liquid (white to yellowish-white) secreted by the mammary glands of mammals after birth; nothing added or taken away.
Cow's milk composition:
• Water: 87.1%
• Lactose: 4.6%
• Milk fat: 4.0%
• Proteins: 3.3% (of which casein 2.6%)
• Minerals: 0.7%
flashcards.explanation: Types include cow, sheep, goat, buffalo, and donkey milk.

flashcards.question: What are the key facts about milk's lactose, fat, proteins and minerals?
flashcards.answer:
Lactose: disaccharide (glucose + galactose); causes lactose intolerance; basis of fermented products.
Milk fat: saturated FA 70% (palmitic, stearic, butyric), MUFA oleic 30-40%, PUFA linoleic 2-3%.
Proteins: biological value higher than meat or fish; casein + whey proteins.
Minerals: potassium (most abundant); Ca:P in favourable ratio 1.2-1.4:1; absorption depends on lactose and vitamin D.
flashcards.explanation: Lactose intolerance is the inability to digest lactose (glucose + galactose).

flashcards.question: How is milk classified by fat content?
flashcards.answer:
• Raw milk: not heated above 40°C
• Whole milk (standardized): at least 3.5% milk fat
• Partial skimmed milk: 1.5-1.8% milk fat
• Skimmed milk: maximum 0.5% milk fat
flashcards.explanation: Standardization adjusts milk fat to a defined level during processing.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between pasteurized and sterilized (UHT) milk?
flashcards.answer:
Pasteurized milk: 72°C for 15-20 seconds ('short-term' pasteurization); shelf life 8-14 days at refrigerator temperature (5°C).
Sterilized milk: UHT (Ultra High Temperature) 135-140°C for a few seconds, filled aseptically into sterile multilayer packaging; shelf life at least 3-4 months at room temperature.
flashcards.explanation: Primary processing also includes filtration, fat standardization, homogenization, and deaeration.

flashcards.question: What happens during the fermentation of milk products?
flashcards.answer:
The main objective is conversion of lactose into lactic acid.
Lactic acid fermentation: by lactic acid bacteria (Streptococcus thermophilus + Lactobacillus) → yogurt, sour milk, acidophilus milk, buttermilk.
Alcoholic fermentation: produces alcohol + CO₂; combined with lactic fermentation it is characteristic of kefir (yeasts + bacteria).
Cultures: mesophilic (20-30°C), thermophilic (37-45°C), therapeutic/probiotic (37-40°C).
flashcards.explanation: Kefir uses kefir grains containing both bacteria and yeasts → milk-acid + alcoholic fermentation.

flashcards.question: What are Greek yogurt, Skyr, and kefir?
flashcards.answer:
Greek-type yogurt: whole milk + cream; higher dry matter and more milk fat (7-10%).
Skyr: traditional Icelandic yogurt; skimmed milk, rennet added; significantly higher protein (~10-11 g/100g vs ~3.5 g/100g in classic yogurt).
Kefir: cooled milk infused with kefir grains (hundreds of bacteria + yeasts), milk-acid + alcoholic fermentation (CO₂ produced); grains are sifted out and reused.
flashcards.explanation: Buttermilk is a by-product of butter production and belongs to fermented milk products.

flashcards.question: What is cheese and how is it classified by fat content?
flashcards.answer:
Cheese: a fresh or matured product made by separating whey after coagulation of milk/cream.
By milk fat in dry matter:
• Extra greasy: ≥60%
• Full-fat: 45-60%
• Greasy: 25-45%
• Semi-fat: 10-25%
• Low fat: <10%
flashcards.explanation: Cheese can be made from cow, goat, sheep, or buffalo milk (or mixtures).

flashcards.question: What are the main steps of cheese production?
flashcards.answer:
1. Standardization (protein-casein ratio)
2. Homogenization (or cream addition)
3. Additives (calcium chloride for curd strength, rennet, enzymes)
4. Adding dairy cultures (lactic acid bacteria)
5. Milk curdling/spreading (~30°C) → cheese curd
6. Curd cutting (whey extraction)
7. Shaping → 8. Pressing → 9. Salting (brine, stops fermentation) → 10. Ripening → 11. Packaging
flashcards.explanation: Rennet and lactic acid bacteria cause the milk to coagulate into curd.

flashcards.question: How are cheeses classified by water content, and name Croatian cheeses.
flashcards.answer:
By water in fat-free substance:
• Extra hard: <51% (Parmesan)
• Hard: 49-56% (Emmental, Cheddar)
• Semi-hard: 54-63% (Gouda, Edam, Trappist)
• Semi-soft: 61-69% (Brie, Gorgonzola)
• Soft: >67% · Fresh: 69-85%
Croatian cheeses: Pag cheese (sheep, 2-5 months, intense), Krk cheese (sheep, mild), Istrian cheese (sheep, 60-120 days), Tounj, Squeak cheese.
flashcards.explanation: Pag cheese is a famous intense, aromatic Croatian sheep's-milk cheese ripened 2-5 months.

flashcards.question: How are butter and ice cream produced?
flashcards.answer:
Butter: from cream (~40% milk fat); butrification = phase inversion turning cream into butter grains, with buttermilk separated; stored at 4-5°C for up to a month.
Ice cream: pasteurized/sterilized milk products + non-dairy ingredients; air is incorporated to increase volume; maturation 2-24 h.
• Creamy ice cream: ≥5% milk fat
• Milky ice cream: ≥2.5% milk fat
Stored frozen at least -15°C, up to one year.
flashcards.explanation: Butrification (churning) is the phase inversion of fat-in-water emulsion into water-in-fat.

flashcards.question: What is an egg and which types are consumed?
flashcards.answer:
An egg is a complex reproductive cell whose structure and composition support the development of new life — sometimes described as an 'organism in miniature'.
Fresh chicken eggs are the most commonly consumed. Eggs may also come from goose, turkey, duck, quail, or ostrich.
Packaging must indicate the type of poultry the eggs originate from.
flashcards.explanation: World egg production is ~83.4 million tons; Asia leads with ~51.9 million tons.

flashcards.question: What is the anatomy of an egg?
flashcards.answer:
• Shell: porous, made of calcium carbonate
• Skin (membrane): on the surface, protects against bacteria
• Airspace: space between two membranes
• Egg white (albumen): two layers — thick and thin
• Chalaza: keeps the yolk in the middle
• Yolk + yolk membrane: yellow, dark and light parts
flashcards.explanation: The chalazae are the twisted strands that hold the yolk centered within the white.

flashcards.question: What is the average chemical composition of a whole egg, yolk, and white?
flashcards.answer:
Whole egg: water 72-75%, protein 12.5-13.3%, fat 10.7-11.6%, carbohydrates 0.7%, minerals 1.0%.
Yolk: water 47-50%, protein 15-17%, fat 28-36%.
White: water 86-88%, protein 10.5-12.3%, fat in traces.
flashcards.explanation: Almost all of the egg's fat is in the yolk; the white is essentially fat-free.

flashcards.question: What is in the egg yolk?
flashcards.answer:
• Fats (65%): monounsaturated (oleic), saturated (palmitic, stearic), polyunsaturated (mainly n-6)
• Phospholipids (31%): lecithin
• Cholesterol (4%)
• Carbohydrates: 0.7-1.4%
• Minerals: iron, phosphorus
• Carotenoids: colour and antioxidants
flashcards.explanation: Lecithin (a phospholipid) makes egg yolk an excellent natural emulsifier.

flashcards.question: What is in the egg white (albumen)?
flashcards.answer:
• Protein of high biological value (BV = 94), essential amino acids, good digestibility
• Avidin: an antinutritive factor
• Minerals: potassium, phosphorus, iron, iodine, copper, cobalt, magnesium, zinc, manganese, calcium
• Vitamins: all except vitamin C
flashcards.explanation: Egg white protein has a biological value of 94 — one of the highest of any food protein.

flashcards.question: How is egg freshness assessed?
flashcards.answer:
• Densitometry: immersion in a 12% salt solution (fresh eggs sink; stale eggs float due to a larger air chamber)
• Candling: examination using an ovoscope (a light source revealing the interior)
flashcards.explanation: As an egg ages, its air chamber grows, so it becomes more buoyant in salt water.

flashcards.question: How are eggs classified by quality and size?
flashcards.answer:
By quality:
• Class A: extra/fresh (for consumers)
• Class B: for industrial processing
By size: S (<53 g), M (53-63 g), L (63-73 g), XL (≥73 g).
Class A requirements: clean undamaged shell; air chamber ≤6 mm (≤4 mm for 'extra'); clear compact white; yolk centered.
flashcards.explanation: An 'extra' Class A egg must have an air chamber no larger than 4 mm.

flashcards.question: What do the egg farming codes mean?
flashcards.answer:
The first digit on an egg indicates the farming method:
• 0 = organic eggs
• 1 = free-range eggs
• 2 = barn / floor farming
• 3 = cage (battery) farming
EU welfare standards for enriched cages (more space, nests, perches, litter) apply from 1 January 2012.
flashcards.explanation: Code 0 = organic; code 3 = cage farming — useful for menu transparency in hospitality.

flashcards.question: How are eggs stored and what egg products exist?
flashcards.answer:
Storage: eggs are mainly consumed fresh; the sale period must not exceed 21 days after laying (summer ~10 days, winter ~21 days). Eggs easily absorb foreign odours — don't store with strong-smelling foods.
Egg products: liquid chilled, frozen liquid, dried, and boiled egg products.
flashcards.explanation: Because eggs readily pick up odours, they should be stored away from pungent foods.

flashcards.question: What are the health benefits and risks of egg consumption?
flashcards.answer:
Benefits: high nutritional density, high biological-value protein, lowering blood pressure, anti-inflammatory effects, antioxidant action, improved bioavailability of certain minerals.
Risks: contamination with Salmonella and Campylobacter bacteria (shell contamination after laying or through the shell), allergic reactions.
flashcards.explanation: Proper handling and storage prevent Salmonella and Campylobacter contamination — critical in hospitality.

learn.title: Lecture 13 – Eggs
learn.content:
🥚 The Egg

A complex reproductive cell — an 'organism in miniature'. Most common = chicken; also goose, turkey, duck, quail, ostrich. World production ~83.4 Mt (Asia leads).

🔬 Anatomy

  • Shell: porous, calcium carbonate
  • Membrane (skin): protects against bacteria
  • Airspace: between two membranes (grows as egg ages)
  • Albumen (white): thick + thin layers
  • Chalaza: keeps yolk centered
  • Yolk + yolk membrane

📊 Composition

ComponentWholeYolkWhite
Water72-75%47-50%86-88%
Protein12.5-13.3%15-17%10.5-12.3%
Fat10.7-11.6%28-36%trace

Yolk: fats 65%, phospholipids 31% (lecithin = emulsifier), cholesterol 4%, iron, carotenoids.
White: protein BV = 94, avidin (antinutritive), all vitamins except C.

🔍 Freshness & Market Classes

  • Densitometry: immersion in 12% salt solution (fresh sinks)
  • Candling: ovoscope examination
QualitySizeFarming code
Class A (fresh) · Class B (industrial)S <53 · M 53-63 · L 63-73 · XL ≥73 g0 organic · 1 free-range · 2 barn · 3 cage

Class A: air chamber ≤6 mm (≤4 mm for 'extra'). Sale period ≤21 days.

🩺 Health

Benefits: high nutritional density, high-BV protein, lowers blood pressure, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant.

Risks: Salmonella & Campylobacter contamination, allergic reactions. Eggs are a key hotel breakfast ingredient — handling and storage are essential.

flashcards.question: What is a healthy diet and what are its three principles?
flashcards.answer:
A healthy (balanced) diet provides an adequate intake and ratio of macronutrients meeting energy and physiological needs (without excess), with sufficient micronutrients and fluids.
Principles:
1. Variety: combining food groups for nutritional synergy (legumes + cereals; non-heme iron + vitamin C)
2. Moderation: of fats, added sugar, salt, alcohol, energy
3. Balance: 85% nutrient-dense foods : 15% 'discretionary calories'
flashcards.explanation: Nutritional synergy means combining foods so nutrients enhance each other (e.g., vitamin C boosts non-heme iron absorption).

flashcards.question: What are the WHO dietary recommendations?
flashcards.answer:
• Total fat: ≤30% of daily energy
• Saturated fatty acids: <10% of energy
• Cholesterol: <300 mg/day
• Carbohydrates: 55-75% of energy
• Added sugars: <10% of energy (≈50 g)
• Protein: 10-15% of energy
• Salt: <5 g/day
• Fruit & vegetables: ≥400 g/day
• Dietary fibre: ≥25 g/day
flashcards.explanation: WHO also targets a 30% reduction in population salt intake by 2025.

flashcards.question: How is nutritional status classified by Body Mass Index (BMI)?
flashcards.answer:
• <18.5 — Malnutrition
• 18.5-24.9 — Normal nutrition
• 25.0-29.9 — Overweight
• 30.0-34.9 — Obesity Grade 1
• 35.0-39.9 — Obesity Grade 2
• >40 — Obesity Grade 3
flashcards.explanation: BMI is a rough indicator of energy balance, but not of macro-/micronutrient adequacy.

flashcards.question: What are the three components of energy expenditure?
flashcards.answer:
1. Basal metabolic rate (BMR): minimum energy to sustain life (respiration, circulation, etc.) — 60-75% of total expenditure.
2. Thermic effect of food (TEF): energy used to digest food — on average ~10% (highest for protein 15-30%, carbs 5-8%, fats 2-3%).
3. Thermic effect of physical activity: the most variable component (100-3000 kcal/day) — 10-35% of total.
flashcards.explanation: BMR is the largest component of daily energy expenditure (60-75%).

flashcards.question: What are the acceptable macronutrient intake ranges?
flashcards.answer:
• Protein: 10-35% of energy (recommended ~10% for an adult; the upper range is for replenishment)
• Carbohydrates: 45-65% (recommended ~60%; ~300 g/day on 2000 kcal)
• Fats: 20-35% (recommended ~30%; ~67 g/day)
• Added sugars: ≤25% (≤500 kcal)
flashcards.explanation: On a 2000 kcal diet: ~50 g protein, ~300 g carbs, ~67 g fat.

flashcards.question: How did dietary guideline graphics evolve?
flashcards.answer:
• Food Guide Pyramid (USDA, 1992): optimal servings from each food group.
• MyPyramid (2005): added a physical-activity symbol (person on stairs), measured in cups/ounces.
• MyPlate (2011-): a plate divided into food groups — a simple visual of what and how much to eat.
flashcards.explanation: Food groups were invented as a public-health tool to prevent nutrient deficiencies and now address chronic diseases too.

flashcards.question: What are the main food groups in MyPlate?
flashcards.answer:
• Fruits (whole preferred over juice)
• Vegetables (5 subgroups: dark green; red & orange; beans/peas/lentils; starchy; other)
• Grains (whole = bran+germ+endosperm; refined = milled, less fibre/iron/B-vitamins)
• Protein foods (seafood, meat/poultry/eggs, beans, nuts/soy — the 'protein package')
• Dairy (milk, yogurt, cheese, fortified soy; excludes butter, cream, cream cheese)
flashcards.explanation: The 'protein package' = all nutrients that come with protein (fats, fibre, sodium) — this is what matters for health.

flashcards.question: What is the Planetary Health plate and the environmental impact of foods?
flashcards.answer:
The Planetary Health plate recommends: half the plate fruits and vegetables (starchy limited), the other half primarily whole grains and plant-based proteins, with unsaturated oils and modest animal-based protein.
Animal foods (especially red meat — beef, lamb, goat) have higher greenhouse-gas emissions than plant foods. Beef accounts for ~36% of US food-related GHG emissions; one pound of lamb generates ~5× the GHG of chicken and ~30× of lentils.
flashcards.explanation: Dairy and especially red meat stand out for their disproportionate environmental impact.

flashcards.question: What are the Mediterranean and DASH diets?
flashcards.answer:
Mediterranean diet: whole grains, varied fruits/vegetables, fibre, low-fat fermented dairy, legumes, olive oil, nuts/seeds, honey for sweetening; eggs and poultry in moderation, red meat occasionally; water + moderate red wine with meals; plus physical activity and social interaction.
DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension): vegetables, fruits, low-fat dairy, whole grains, varied protein; limits added sugar (<10%), saturated fat (<10%), sodium (<2300 mg/day), alcohol.
flashcards.explanation: DASH was designed to lower blood pressure; it strictly limits sodium to <2300 mg/day.

flashcards.question: What are the MIND and Nordic diets, and food/health claims?
flashcards.answer:
MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH for Neurodegenerative Delay): prevents cognitive decline; emphasizes dark leafy greens, nuts, berries, whole grains, fish, poultry, olive oil; avoids red meat, cheese, butter, fried food.
Nordic diet: Nordic foods — green vegetables, berries, fish, whole grains (barley, rye, oats), almonds, β-glucan foods, canola oil; little red meat.
Claims: a nutrition claim states beneficial nutrient content; a health claim links a food/component to health. Front-of-package labels (FoPL) are voluntary.
flashcards.explanation: The MIND diet specifically targets brain health and slowing age-related cognitive decline.

flashcards.question: What is the structure and weight of the Food & Nutrition final exam?
flashcards.answer: The final exam is worth 30% (minimum 15% to pass) and is obligatory. It has 16 questions: 12 with short/suggested answers (1.5% each) + 4 essay-type questions (max 3% each). It covers all material, Topics 1–14.
flashcards.explanation: The prerequisite to take the final is at least 35% from coursework (midterms, seminars, activities).

flashcards.question: Which topics make up the two midterm 'halves' that the final combines?
flashcards.answer:
1st midterm = Topics 1–7: Food Quality, Food Components, Food Preservation, Cereals & Bakery, Fruits & Vegetables, Coffee/Tea/Cocoa, and Wine.
2nd midterm = Topics 8–14: Beer, Distilled Spirits & Liqueurs, Meat, Fish, Milk & Dairy, Eggs, and Healthy Diet.
flashcards.explanation: Per the syllabus, Beer (Topic 8) belongs to the 2nd midterm, not the 1st.

flashcards.question: What are the energy values of the three energy-yielding macronutrients?
flashcards.answer:
Proteins: 4 kcal/g (≈17 kJ/g)
Carbohydrates: 4 kcal/g (≈17 kJ/g)
Fats: 9 kcal/g (≈39 kJ/g)
(1 kcal ≈ 4.187 kJ). Vitamins, minerals, bioactive compounds, and water provide NO energy.
flashcards.explanation: Fat provides more than double the energy per gram of protein or carbohydrate — a recurring exam number.

flashcards.question: Distinguish complete and incomplete proteins and give a hospitality example of combining them.
flashcards.answer: Complete proteins contain all essential amino acids and come from animal origin (meat, milk, eggs, fish). Incomplete proteins (plant origin) have a limiting amino acid. Combining legumes + cereals (≈35:65) creates a complete amino-acid profile.
flashcards.explanation: This 'protein complementation' is the basis of balanced vegetarian menus.

flashcards.question: Compare the key preservation principles and their critical temperatures.
flashcards.answer: ABIOSIS = destroy/remove microorganisms (sterilization >100°C). ANABIOSIS = inhibit them (cooling, freezing, drying, fermentation). Key temps: pasteurization <100°C, sterilization >100°C, blanching 75-95°C, frozen storage -18°C, lyophilization freezes at -50°C.
flashcards.explanation: ABIOSIS eliminates microbes; ANABIOSIS just creates unfavourable conditions for them.

flashcards.question: Rank the alcoholic beverages by minimum alcohol content and state the common reaction.
flashcards.answer: Beer: standard 3.5-5.5% vol. → Wine: ≥8.5% vol. → Distilled spirits & liqueurs: ≥15% vol. (distilled spirits 30-50%; liqueurs also need ≥100 g/L sugar). All rely on alcoholic fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + yeast → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂.
flashcards.explanation: Saccharomyces yeast drives fermentation in bread, beer, wine and spirits alike; distillation then concentrates the spirit's alcohol.

flashcards.question: Name the characteristic stimulant compound of coffee, tea, and cocoa.
flashcards.answer: Coffee → caffeine (stimulates the central nervous and respiratory systems). Tea → theophylline. Cocoa → theobromine (named after Theobroma cacao). Theobromine and theophylline have a milder, relaxing effect.
flashcards.explanation: All three are bioactive alkaloids acting on the central nervous system.

flashcards.question: Summarise the nutritional 'signature' of each animal-origin food group.
flashcards.answer: Meat: 15-20% protein, the best heme-iron source, B12. Fish: omega-3 PUFA (EPA + DHA), low cholesterol. Milk: protein biological value higher than meat/fish, calcium (Ca:P ≈ 1.2-1.4:1). Eggs: egg-white protein has biological value 94 (one of the highest).
flashcards.explanation: Animal foods are complete-protein sources; fish adds heart-protective omega-3s.

flashcards.question: How does fermentation appear across the whole course?
flashcards.answer: Alcoholic fermentation (yeast → alcohol + CO₂): bread, beer, wine, spirits. Lactic-acid fermentation: dairy (yogurt, kefir — kefir is also alcoholic), pickled vegetables (sauerkraut), fermented sausages. Biological preservation of food relies on these microbial processes.
flashcards.explanation: Recognising the type of fermentation per product is a strong cross-topic exam skill.

flashcards.question: Match each food group with its main freshness/quality indicator.
flashcards.answer: Meat: colour from myoglobin (red/white), elastic surface. Fish: clear full eyes, bright-red moist gills, firm flesh; spoilage smell = TMA (trimethylamine). Eggs: densitometry (12% salt solution) and candling (ovoscope). Milk: heat treatment (pasteurization 72°C / UHT 135-140°C).
flashcards.explanation: Each group has its own sensory and instrumental quality tests.

flashcards.question: List the core WHO healthy-diet recommendations.
flashcards.answer: Total fat ≤30% of energy; saturated fat <10%; cholesterol <300 mg/day; carbohydrates 55-75%; added sugars <10% (≈50 g); protein 10-15%; salt <5 g/day; fruit & vegetables ≥400 g/day; dietary fibre ≥25 g/day.
flashcards.explanation: These are the headline numbers from the Healthy Diet topic (Topic 14).

flashcards.question: Explain BMI classification and the components of energy expenditure.
flashcards.answer: BMI: <18.5 malnutrition, 18.5-24.9 normal, 25-29.9 overweight, ≥30 obesity (grades 1/2/3). Energy expenditure = basal metabolic rate (60-75%) + thermic effect of food (~10%) + physical activity (10-35%, the most variable).
flashcards.explanation: BMR is the largest, most stable component of daily energy use.

flashcards.question: Compare the four nutrition models for health promotion.
flashcards.answer: Mediterranean: whole grains, olive oil, fish, legumes, moderate red wine with meals. DASH: stops hypertension; sodium <2300 mg/day. MIND: Mediterranean + DASH for brain health (greens, berries, nuts, fish). Nordic: Nordic foods, berries, oats/barley (β-glucan), canola oil.
flashcards.explanation: All four emphasise plants, whole grains and healthy fats while limiting red meat.

flashcards.question: What are the main food-safety hazards across the animal-origin foods?
flashcards.answer: Meat: putrefaction → toxic biogenic amines. Fish: histamine (histidine→histamine by bacteria) and the Anisakis parasite (raw fish/sushi). Eggs: Salmonella and Campylobacter. Overarching principle: traceability — 'one step forward, one step back' / 'from farm to fork'.
flashcards.explanation: Food safety is a prerequisite for food quality — a key Topic 1 concept that recurs throughout.

learn.title: Final Exam Roadmap (Topics 1–14)
learn.content:
📋 What the Final Covers

The final exam is worth 30% (minimum 15% to pass) and is obligatory; the prerequisite to sit it is at least 35% from coursework. It has 16 questions: 12 short/suggested-answer (1.5% each) + 4 essay-type (max 3% each), covering all 14 topics.

Use this category to drill across topics; the 14 per-topic categories remain available in this same lesson for deep revision.

🍽️ First Midterm Half — Topics 1–7

TopicMust-know anchor
1. Food QualityEnergy 4/4/9 kcal/g; objective vs subjective methods; "farm to fork"
2. Food ComponentsComplete vs incomplete proteins; GI <55/56-69/>70; fat- vs water-soluble vitamins
3. Food PreservationABIOSIS vs ANABIOSIS; pasteurization <100°C / sterilization >100°C; -18°C
4. Cereals & BakeryGluten = gliadin + glutelin; flour type = ash × 1000; celiac disease
5. Fruits & VegetablesPulses 18-35% protein; lycopene = red; jam 35g / extra jam 45g; ≥400 g/day
6. Coffee/Tea/CocoaArabica 70% / Robusta 30%; caffeine/theophylline/theobromine; conching
7. Wine≥8.5% vol; anthocyanins; malolactic fermentation; Champagne vs Charmat

🍺 Second Midterm Half — Topics 8–14

TopicMust-know anchor
8. BeerMalt + water + yeast + hops; lager (bottom) vs ale (top); EBC; ~45 kcal/100ml
9. Distilled Spirits & Liqueurs≥15% vol; fermentation creates + distillation concentrates; liqueurs ≥100 g/L sugar
10. MeatWater 65-75%; heme-iron; putrefaction → biogenic amines; freeze -18°C
11. FishLean <3% / fatty >8% fat; EPA + DHA (omega-3); TMA = spoilage; 2 servings/week
12. Milk & DairyWater 87%; lactose = glucose + galactose; pasteurization 72°C / UHT 135-140°C
13. EggsShell = CaCO₃; white BV = 94; avidin; codes 0-3; Salmonella
14. Healthy DietWHO: fat ≤30%, salt <5g, fibre ≥25g; BMI; BMR 60-75%; Mediterranean/DASH/MIND

🔗 Cross-Topic Threads

  • Fermentation everywhere: alcoholic (bread, beer, wine, spirits) vs lactic-acid (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, sausages).
  • Alcohol ladder: beer 3.5-5.5% → wine ≥8.5% → spirits/liqueurs ≥15% (distilled 30-50%).
  • Food safety: putrefaction (meat), histamine + Anisakis (fish), Salmonella (eggs); traceability "one step forward, one step back".
  • Protein quality: animal = complete; combine legumes + cereals for a complete plant profile.

💡 Exam Strategy

Short questions reward exact numbers and definitions (energy values, temperatures, percentages, alcohol minimums). Essay questions reward a concept + an example (e.g. "ANABIOSIS → refrigerating fish at <4°C slows microbial growth", or "complete protein → combine beans with rice"). Revise one strong anchor per topic, then practise linking topics.
